0.name: Hay Heghapokhakan Dashnaktsutyun
0.text:
The Dashnaktsutyun, founded in Tiflis in 1890, governed the independent Republic of Armenia in 1918-1920 and has been outlawed on Soviet soil since the Bolsheviks took Yerevan. On 1 January 1970 it is the strongest organisation of the Armenian diaspora, directed by a Bureau in Beirut, with mass bases in Lebanon, Syria, Iran, France and the United States, the newspapers Aztag and Hairenik and the Armenian Youth Federation.

Its programme remains a free, independent and united Armenia including the provinces held by Turkey, and it treats Soviet rule as occupation. In the Cold War this has made it a partner of the West: it backed Camille Chamoun in Lebanon's 1958 crisis and stands behind the Catholicosate of Cilicia in Antelias against Etchmiadzin. Its leverage is money, discipline and a dense web of schools, clubs and scouts that keeps the exiles hostile to Moscow.

1.name: Ramgavar Azatakan Kusaktsutyun
1.text:
The Ramgavar Party was formed in Constantinople in 1921 by the merger of the Armenakan Party, the Reformed Hnchaks and the Armenian Constitutional Democrats. Banned in Soviet Armenia, it lives in the communities of Beirut, Cairo, Aleppo, Boston and Paris, where its merchants, doctors and lawyers publish Zartonk and Baikar and sit on the boards of the Armenian General Benevolent Union.

Its creed is bourgeois liberalism wrapped in patriotism: private property, parliamentary politics, respect for the Church and loyalty to the existing Armenian homeland whatever its regime. Since the 1940s it has backed repatriation and cultural ties with Soviet Armenia and sided with Etchmiadzin against the Dashnaks, while its members vote for Western parties at home. Inside the republic its appeal lies with families that have relatives abroad and with a respectable, church-going middle class.

2.name: Akhparner
2.text:
Akhpar, Western Armenian for 'brother', is what Yerevan calls the roughly 100,000 diaspora Armenians who answered Stalin's call during the Great Repatriation of 1946-1949. Arriving from Lebanon, Syria, Greece, France, Iran and the Americas, they met suspicion, housing shortages and, in 1949, deportations to the Altai. By 1970 they form a distinct milieu, at home in French and Arabic as well as Armenian, without an organisation, a newspaper or a recognised leader.

The Akhpars want what the Soviet system rations: the right to travel and to emigrate, letters and parcels from relatives abroad, Western records and clothes, and a state that treats citizens as individuals. Pro-Western without being anti-Armenian, they press quietly for exit visas and contacts with the outside world. Their leverage is economic skill and foreign ties: they dominate tailoring, shoemaking and jewellery trades and link the republic to its emigrants.

3.name: Garuni Serund
3.text:
Garun ('Spring'), a Yerevan literary and social monthly launched in 1967 and edited by the writer Vardges Petrosyan, has become the platform of a generation that came of age in the Thaw. Its pages carry bold prose, frank debates about history and a sympathy for reform communism that the censors watch nervously. The circle around it is no party but a network of young writers, journalists, scientists and Komsomol cadres.

Its members want socialism with a human face: an end to censorship, honest history including 1915 and the purges, elected rather than appointed managers and more autonomy for the republic within the Union. They are not anti-Soviet and look to the Czechoslovak and Yugoslav experiments rather than to Washington. Their leverage lies in the universities, the Writers' Union and the press, where they shape the language educated Armenians use about their future.

4.name: Hayastani Komunistakan Kusaktsutyun
4.text:
The Communist Party of Armenia, founded in 1920 and a republican branch of the CPSU, holds a monopoly of power in the Armenian SSR. Its First Secretary since February 1966 is Anton Kochinyan, the long-serving former premier installed after Moscow removed Yakov Zarobyan, whose tolerance of the national mood around the 1965 genocide anniversary had alarmed the Kremlin. Badal Muradyan heads the Council of Ministers and Nagush Harutyunyan the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet.

The party governs a small, fast-industrialising republic of 2.5 million people, building chemical works, power stations and electronics plants while sanctioning memorials such as Tsitsernakaberd and Sardarapat to channel national feeling. Kochinyan's line is loyalty to Brezhnev, cautious patronage of Armenian culture and firm suppression of open nationalism. Its leverage is total: the nomenklatura, the press, the courts and the security organs all answer to its Central Committee.

5.name: Hayastani Leninyan Komunistakan Eritasardakan Miutyun
5.english: Leninist Young Communist League of Armenia
5.text:
The Armenian Komsomol organises nearly every student, young worker and junior officer in the republic and serves as the training school of the next nomenklatura. As Lenin's centenary year opens, its activists lead shock brigades on construction sites, student building detachments in the virgin lands and solidarity rallies for Vietnam and Cuba.

A restless radical wing inside it is tired of careerism and bureaucratic ritual. Its young militants idolise Che Guevara and the Bolsheviks of 1917, demand that privileges be cut and corruption punished, and want a return to revolutionary enthusiasm and internationalism. Firmly pro-Soviet and anti-American, they would rather purify the system than change it. Their leverage is numbers, energy and access to every school, institute and factory in the republic.

6.name: Bolshevikyan Hin Gvardia
6.text:
The Bolshevik Old Guard gathers the hardline veterans of the party, state and security apparatus formed under Stalin and Beria. Many rose in the purge year of 1937, served the long regime of First Secretary Grigory Arutyunov until 1953 and never accepted the rehabilitations and the Thaw. They are pensioners, district secretaries, ideologists and procurators rather than an organised faction.

They regard the 1965 genocide rallies, the new memorials and the popularity of national poets as dangerous concessions to Dashnak nationalism. They want strict ideological discipline, renewed atheist campaigns against Etchmiadzin, the restoration of Stalin's good name and a stern line on emigre contacts. Unconditionally loyal to Moscow and hostile to the West, they find allies in the central apparatus that has grown wary since Khrushchev's fall and in parts of the security organs.

7.name: Haykakan SSH Petakan Anvtangutyan Komite
7.english: Committee for State Security of the Armenian SSR
7.text:
The Committee for State Security of the Armenian SSR is the republic branch of the Soviet KGB, headquartered in Yerevan and led since 1954 by Georgy Badamyants, one of the longest-serving security chiefs in the Union. It watches the repatriates, the clergy of Etchmiadzin, the universities and every contact with the diaspora, and in 1968-1969 it broke up the underground National United Party.

As a power bloc it stands for order before ideology: tight control of emigration, informers in every institute, the struggle against Dashnak influence and a sealed border with NATO's Turkey. Answering to Moscow as much as to the local party, it can make or break careers and holds files on the whole Armenian elite. Its leverage is information, the power of arrest and a direct line to Yuri Andropov's headquarters at the Lubyanka.

8.name: Zängibasar Ağsaqqalları
8.text:
Zangibasar, the cluster of Azerbaijani villages in the Masis district just south of Yerevan, is the heart of the roughly 150,000 Azerbaijanis living in the Armenian SSR. With almost every mosque shut and no registered clergy, religious life is kept by village elders, the white-bearded agsaqqals who organise Muharram mourning, weddings and burials and settle disputes far from the party's eyes.

The elders seek a modest, legal space for Shia faith: a reopened mosque or two, Azerbaijani-language schooling, protection of village land and dignity for a minority uneasy in a republic shaped by the memory of 1915. They avoid open politics, cooperate with collective-farm chairmen and look to Baku and to the shrines of Iran for guidance. Their leverage is cohesion: tight kinship networks, the loyalty of whole villages and links to relatives in Nakhichevan.

9.name: Vedibasar Mollaları
9.text:
In the Vedi valley near the Nakhichevan border, where Azerbaijani villages stand beside Armenian ones, a few unregistered mullahs keep the madrasa learning of their fathers alive. They teach the Koran and Persian prayers to boys in private homes, marry couples by Shia rite and revere the great marjas of Najaf and Qom, whose names reach them through Tabriz radio and rare pilgrims.

They reject Soviet atheism outright and regard the official Baku board as servants of the state. Their ideal is a community ruled by the sharia and guided by a learned mujtahid, an idea that exiled clerics such as Ruhollah Khomeini now preach openly in Najaf. They have no weapons and few followers, but in a crisis their sermons, Ashura processions and authority over marriage and inheritance could turn quiet piety into defiance.

10.name: Göy Mäscid Camaatı
10.text:
The Blue Mosque, built in the 1760s under the khans of Erivan, is the last great Muslim monument of Yerevan; since the 1930s it has housed a city museum. Around its memory gathers the loyal Azerbaijani establishment of the capital: teachers of the Azerbaijani schools, journalists of the newspaper Sovet Ermänistanı, actors of the Azerbaijani theatre and the few believers who correspond with the Spiritual Board of the Muslims of Transcaucasia in Baku.

This milieu is Muslim by culture and Soviet by career. It asks only for what the law allows: a registered prayer house, a representative of the Baku board, permission for pilgrimages and respect for Muslim cemeteries. Its members denounce both underground mullahs and foreign propaganda and present themselves as proof that Soviet nationality policy works. Their leverage lies in party cards, access to Baku's leadership and their role as mediators for the Azerbaijani villages.

11.name: Halqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
Among the Arab students sent to Yerevan's university and medical institute under Soviet friendship programmes are a few Jordanians and Palestinians who brought with them the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. They meet in dormitory rooms, pass around hand-copied pamphlets and pray together on Fridays in a city without a working mosque.

They hold that nationalism, socialism and Western democracy alike are idols, and that only a restored caliphate governing by the sharia can unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. They despise both the Soviet hosts who pay their stipends and the Arab regimes that sent them. Isolated, watched by the KGB and without roots among local Muslims, the circle has no leverage beyond its conviction and the contacts its members will carry home.

12.name: Usrat al-Talaba al-Muslimin
12.text:
Syrian and Egyptian students in Yerevan include young men raised in the milieu of the Muslim Brotherhood, which Ba'athist Damascus and Nasser's Cairo have driven underground. Organised in a small usra, the Brotherhood's cell of mutual study and support, they read Hasan al-Banna and Mustafa al-Siba'i, fast during Ramadan together and seek out Azerbaijani families in the Ararat valley for halal meat and hospitality.

Unlike the caliphate radicals they favour gradual reform: personal piety first, then Islamic education, charity and a constitutional state guided by the sharia. They are anti-communist but cautious, aiming to finish their degrees and return home as doctors and engineers with a mission. In Armenia their leverage is negligible beyond a few friendships, but they form a bridge between local Muslims and the wider Islamic revival.

13.name: Haykakan SSH Ministrneri Khorhurd
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Armenian SSR
13.text:
The Council of Ministers is the republic's government, a pyramid of ministries, state committees and the Armenian Gosplan that runs factories, farms, construction and supply. Since 1966 it has been chaired by Badal Muradyan, and it works closely with the Academy of Sciences under the astrophysicist Viktor Hambardzumyan and with the directors of Yerevan's electronics, chemical and machine-building plants.

As a faction it stands for management over mobilisation: plan targets met, investment won from Moscow, computer and instrument factories, hydroelectric dams and the planned nuclear power station, and pragmatic toleration of whatever keeps output rising. It has little interest in ideology, in the Cold War or in national passions and prefers expertise to slogans. Its leverage is control of budgets, housing and jobs, and the dependence of every district on its allocations.

14.name: Mayr Ator Surb Echmiadzin
14.text:
The Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin, the ancient seat of the Catholicos of All Armenians, is the only Armenian national institution older than the Soviet state that still functions inside it. Since 1955 it has been led by Vazgen I, a teacher from the Armenian community of Bucharest whom Moscow allows to restore churches, train priests and travel to Armenian communities abroad.

The church preaches continuity: faith, family, language and the memory of 1915, kept alive within the limits of Soviet law. Vazgen avoids open confrontation, praises peace and the homeland and serves Soviet diplomacy abroad, yet every baptism and pilgrimage to Etchmiadzin is a quiet vote for Armenian identity. It is neither Western nor Soviet in spirit. Its leverage is moral authority over Armenians everywhere, despite the rival See of Cilicia in Antelias.

15.name: Haykakan Baregortsakan Endhanur Miutyun
15.text:
The Armenian General Benevolent Union was founded in Cairo in 1906 by Boghos Nubar Pasha and is the richest institution of the Armenian diaspora. Its president since 1953 is Alex Manoogian, a Detroit industrialist whose fortune comes from the Masco faucet company, and its councils unite bankers, industrialists and merchants from New York to Beirut and Buenos Aires.

The Union funds schools, scholarships, hospitals and cultural projects and cultivates good relations with Etchmiadzin and Soviet Armenia, sponsoring church restoration and cultural exchanges with Moscow's blessing. Its politics are those of capital and patronage: stability, private philanthropy and influence through money rather than parties, with sympathy for the Ramgavar liberals. Inside the republic its leverage is foreign currency, prestige and the gifts and projects that leading officials are glad to accept.

16.name: Yerevani Tsekhavikner
16.text:
Behind the facades of state factories and cooperatives, Yerevan hosts one of the busiest shadow economies of the Soviet Union. Its tsekhaviks, managers and private operators of unofficial workshops, turn diverted materials into shoes, knitwear, jewellery and plastics sold across the Union, while craftsmen and kolkhoz traders keep the markets full of goods the plan never delivers.

They want what they already practise: freedom to produce, to hire, to set prices and to keep profits, with fewer inspections and lighter planning. They have no programme and no leaders who could be named in public, but they buy protection from officials, militia and prosecutors and finance weddings, houses and careers. In a reform they would be the first private entrepreneurs; under current law they risk the death penalty for large-scale theft of socialist property.

17.name: Prkenk Sevane
17.text:
Lake Sevan, the great alpine lake of Armenia, has been drained since the 1930s for irrigation and the Sevan-Hrazdan hydropower cascade. Its level has fallen by some eighteen metres, exposing islands, shrinking fish stocks and threatening the water itself. Scientists of the Academy of Sciences, writers and fishermen have turned the lake into a national cause, and in the 1960s work began on the Arpa-Sevan tunnel to feed it.

The defenders of Sevan want an end to the drawdown, priority for the lake over power targets, protection of the ishkhan trout and a wider respect for nature that they present as patriotism. They criticise planners rather than the party and work through petitions, newspaper articles and scientific commissions. Their leverage is public emotion: few issues unite Armenians so easily as the image of a dying blue lake.

18.name: Sotsial-Demokrat Hnchakyan Kusaktsutyun
18.text:
Founded in Geneva in 1887 by Armenian students around Avetis Nazarbekian, the Hnchak party was the first socialist party in the Ottoman and Persian lands. Never a governing force, it survived the genocide and the Soviet takeover in the diaspora, where it is active in Beirut, Aleppo, Cairo and the United States with its own clubs, schools and newspapers.

Since the 1920s the Hnchaks have regarded Soviet Armenia as the realised homeland and defend it against the Dashnaks, while keeping their own Marxist but non-Leninist social-democratic identity. They call for social justice, welfare for workers and refugees, recognition of the genocide and the recovery of lost lands through Soviet power. Their leverage lies among the diaspora's working poor and in their usefulness to Moscow as friendly socialists outside the CPSU.

19.name: Khanjyanakanner
19.text:
Aghasi Khanjian, First Secretary from 1930 until he was killed in Beria's office in 1936, is the hero of Armenia's national communists: officials and intellectuals loyal to socialism who insist that it must serve the Armenian nation. Their high point came in 1965, when the party under Yakov Zarobyan let the fiftieth anniversary of the genocide be marked and approved the Tsitsernakaberd memorial; Zarobyan's removal in 1966 pushed them back into the shadows.

They want more autonomy for Yerevan, Armenian-language schooling and history, Karabakh and Nakhichevan joined to the republic and recognition of the genocide in Soviet foreign policy. Titoist in temperament, they keep their distance from Moscow centralisers and Western-backed emigres alike. Their leverage lies in district committees, the Writers' Union and the Academy, and in poets such as Silva Kaputikyan and Paruyr Sevak who give voice to their feelings.

20.name: Azgayin Miatsyal Kusaktsutyun
20.text:
The National United Party was founded underground in Yerevan on 24 April 1966, the anniversary of the genocide, by the painter Haykaz Khachatryan, Stepan Zatikyan and Shahen Harutyunyan. Its founders were arrested in 1968, and the student Paruyr Hayrikyan, who took over the leadership, was seized by the KGB in March 1969. On 1 January 1970 it survives as a few cells of young workers and students while its leaders sit in prison.

Its programme, 'For the Nation and the Homeland', demands an independent and democratic Armenia, redress for the genocide and the reunification of the Armenian lands held by Turkey and Azerbaijan. It spreads leaflets, honours the martyrs of 1915 and treats Russian rule and Turkish denial as twin enemies. Its leverage is moral rather than material: the nationalist mood of Armenian youth since the rallies of 1965.

21.name: Nzhdehakanner
21.text:
Garegin Nzhdeh, hero of the 1919-1921 fighting in Zangezur, preached tseghakronutyun, a creed that made the Armenian nation a sacred racial and religious community, and in 1933 founded the Tseghakron movement among American Armenians. Compromised by his wartime dealings with Germany, he died in Vladimir prison in 1955, but his cult lives on among militant diaspora youth in Beirut, Boston and Paris.

His followers despise both communism and liberal democracy and dream of a militarised Armenia led by a heroic elite that will avenge 1915 and reconquer the lost provinces by arms. They are few, scattered and distrusted even by the Dashnak leadership. Their leverage lies in romance and violence: martial youth camps, the songs of Zangezur and a readiness for armed action that the older parties no longer offer.

22.name: Sparapetner
22.text:
The Sparapets, named after the supreme commanders of the ancient Armenian kingdoms, are the Armenian officers of the Soviet armed forces. The republic has given the Union a remarkable military elite: Marshal Ivan Bagramyan, wartime front commander and now a general inspector of the Ministry of Defence, Marshal of Armoured Troops Hamazasp Babajanyan, head of the tank forces, and dozens of generals. On Armenian soil the 7th Guards Army, headquartered in Yerevan, guards the Turkish frontier.

These soldiers are Soviet patriots first, but they share a conviction that Armenia's survival depends on armed strength and discipline, and they distrust both party windbags and nationalist hotheads. In a crisis they would favour rule by officers, harsh order, a fortified border with NATO's Turkey and generous defence industry for the republic. Their leverage is prestige, the garrisons and the veterans' networks that revere Bagramyan.

23.name: Casa Savoia
23.text:
When Levon V, the last king of Cilician Armenia, died in exile in Paris in 1393, his title passed to the Lusignan kings of Cyprus, and in 1485 Queen Charlotte of Cyprus ceded her claims to the House of Savoy. Ever since, the Savoyards have styled themselves kings of Cyprus, Jerusalem and Armenia. In 1970 the claim rests with Umberto II, the last king of Italy, in exile at Cascais in Portugal since 1946.

For most Armenians the claim is a curiosity rather than a cause. Yet it offers a romantic monarchist option: a Christian, European dynasty linked to the Cilician kingdom, standing above both commissars and Dashnak revolutionaries and able to call on the goodwill of Europe's Catholic and conservative elites. Umberto's leverage is slight: a historic name, a court in exile and the sympathy of royalists across the continent.
